extracted.subtask_description: Composing concise, datelined wire-service news dispatches (especially wartime reporting) that summarize events, attribute sources, and provide precise factual details for a broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and agency tag
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin stories with a dateline showing city and date plus agency attribution, e.g., "MOSCOW, Sept. 12 (A. P.).—".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include the location and date up front and, for wire copy, the agency abbreviation in parentheses. This orients the reader and indicates the report's origin (examples throughout: MOSCOW, LONDON, CAIRO datelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise lead summarizing who/what/when/why
rubrics_metrics.description: First sentence should state the main fact succinctly — who did what, when and why (example: "United States Ambassador Laurence A. Steinhardt returned ... after a four-month round-the-world trip to Washington to report to President Roosevelt.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pack the most newsworthy facts into the lede so readers get the gist immediately; follow with supporting detail in subsequent paragraphs (classic inverted-pyramid practice visible across items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute claims to named sources and official communiqués
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports consistently identify the origin of claims — named agencies, officials, or communiqués (e.g., "Tass, official Russian news agency, reported...", "Air Ministry-Home Security Ministry communique").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting contested or military events, explicitly attribute to the reporting agency or named official/communique rather than presenting unverifiable assertions as fact; quote agency names and communique titles where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of BULLETIN/breaking-update labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking or updated information is flagged with labels like "BULLETIN" or similar headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark urgent updates clearly so editors and readers can identify late-breaking changes; examples show bulletins inserted amid dispatches for fresh developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include precise numeric details (casualties, tonnage, ship names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories supply exact figures and identifiers when known — numbers killed/injured, tonnage, ship names and sizes (e.g., "Ville de Mons, 7,430 tons", "four tankers built in Russia").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify events with units and proper names where possible; such specifics increase credibility. When numbers are uncertain, indicate estimates or source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic precision and theatre detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Place names and geographic routes are specific and often multi-level (river, city, region), e.g., "Dnieper River via Kiev", "Tempelhof airdrome", "Mersa Matruh".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give exact locations and geographic context (theater, nearby landmarks, routes) so readers understand where events occurred and their strategic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short paragraphs and inverted-pyramid structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy is broken into brief paragraphs; most important facts appear early followed by supporting detail and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short for readability in wire copy; use the inverted pyramid to allow editors to truncate from the bottom without losing the main facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral, factual tone with clear separation of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: News dispatches maintain an objective, factual tone; opinion or interpretive columns are labeled by author (e.g., Dewitt Mackenzie column) and set apart from straight reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid editorializing in news items; place analysis or commentary in clearly identified columns or bylines so readers can distinguish fact from interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid direct quotations for eyewitness color
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotes from participants or witnesses are used for immediacy and color (examples: pilots' remarks: "FIRES ARE BLAZING ALL OVER THE PLACE...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve quotations for authoritative voices or striking eyewitness details; use them to convey emotional impact or firsthand observation while attributing source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical military/naval terminology for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports use specific military and naval terms (E-boats, U-boat, anti-aircraft barrage, tonnage, convoy) and describe tactics and effects (barrage screens, parachute flares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ accepted technical terms to convey operational detail accurately; when necessary clarify or define for lay readers but preserve precision in describing actions and equipment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize multiple datelines for broader narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The page aggregates dispatches from many cities (Moscow, London, Cairo, Rome, Berlin) to present a wide-ranging, multi-front account of developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering large events (e.g., wartime activity) compile and cross-reference reports from several locations to give readers a comprehensive picture and note differing accounts or attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interleave human-interest/social items with hard news
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside military and diplomatic dispatches the copy includes society and human-interest pieces (donations, visits by royalty, refugee stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance front-line coverage with human-interest or domestic items to retain broader readership engagement; keep such items factual and clearly labeled as society/feature news.
